baer-heitev.1#א: And meat—Shach wrote: this means even where the slaughterers are Israelite; and it is difficult regarding what is said in the Gemara, siman 63, that if meat was in a non-Jew's hand where most sellers are Israelites it is kosher—one should distinguish: there it deals with meat found in a non-Jew's hand that they bought from the market, where there is no concern he bought nevelah and no concern he switched with nevelah in his house—for what purpose would he switch; but here it deals with sending or depositing in a non-Jew's hand where there is concern he switched with nevelah he still has, and moreover it stays a long time with him and he has opportunity to switch—unlike there, buying from the market; and see siman 128. Nevertheless, with seal within seal for Torah prohibitions and one seal for rabbinic prohibitions, it is permitted even l'chatchila to send via a non-Jew; and what the Mechaber wrote "deposited," etc.—the language of b'dieved is not precise; and so the Mechaber wrote explicitly in siman 130—it is simple; and as with a non-Jew, so with a suspect Israelite in this matter, end of his words—see there where he elaborated somewhat.
baer-heitev.1#ב: Honey—Shach wrote: it must deal with mixing so much honey that the wine's taste changed, for then there is no stam yeinam concern—see siman 123; and what he wrote "and likewise vinegar" means vinegar of wine, when it bubbles as thrown on the ground, then it is full vinegar unfit for libation, and if so why concern—if for affection of libation it is unfit for libation; if lest he switch with stam yeinam vinegar, since stam yeinam is only d'rabbanan we are not concerned and one seal suffices; and the same for morayes, cooked wine, and wine mixed with other things—they suffice with one seal. And see there siman 6; and milk: even though concern he switched with impure milk which is d'oraisa—impure milk is recognizable as turbid, so no concern he switched all or most, only perhaps a little which is only d'rabbanan, for min b'mino is nullified in majority from the Torah; and morayes: concern he switched with their morayes forbidden where they put wine in it, as siman 114, seif 1; but where they do not put wine, or wine is dearer than morayes, clearly no seal needed; and bread: obviously where they practice leniency with non-Jewish bread no seal is needed. (And Peri Chadash wrote: even where they practice leniency with pat palter, a seal is needed lest they switch with pat baal habayit forbidden everywhere.) And cheese: even though concern he switched with their cheese forbidden because they curdle with nevelah stomach lining—d'oraisa the lining is nullified in minority, and what is not nullified is d'rabbanan; or the main concern is perhaps he curdled with herbs and still forbidden lest he curdled with nevelah lining—it is properly d'rabbanan—understand, end of Shach.
baer-heitev.1#ג: And some say—and below siman 130 the Mechaber states the first view without a disputant—and understand.
baer-heitev.1#ד: Informed him—Shach wrote: the same if he does not inform his fellow but tells the non-Jew he informed—he still fears, for he thinks it is true; all this follows the second view, unlike the first—and understand; nevertheless even when sending with two seals it is proper to inform the fellow the seal's form so he will inspect afterward.
baer-heitev.1#ה: Suspect—for this matter he is worse than a non-Jew who is trusted they will believe him and does not fear much; it deals with one suspect to switch—not suspect to eat what he sends, for we hold one suspect to eat forbidden things is not suspect to switch them; perhaps those things the public are not lenient about—he is also suspect to switch if suspect to eat them, as the Mechaber writes in siman 119; but the Rashba wrote eating non-Jewish cheese is lenient in the public's eyes, and so the Tur in that siman: one suspect regarding cheese is not suspect to switch, end of Shach; and the Taz ruled that with a non-Jew one seal suffices and a lock counts as a seal (and Nachalat Shiva objected that a lock only helps where two seals are needed, then lock and seal suffice, but not where only one seal is needed—see there).
baer-heitev.2#א: Two—and likewise more; and below siman 130, seif 8, the Rav set conditions on this—see there, Shach.
baer-heitev.2#ב: Through contact—Taz wrote: the explanation is that with wine there is concern even if clear he did not drink from it—e.g., guards outside prevented bringing water to mix, and we see nothing missing from its measure—still concern because of contact even without benefit, lest while occupied (because of affection of libation) he touched the wine, as the Rama wrote in siman 128, seif 4; and this is forbidden even for us, unlike the Levush—see there.
baer-heitev.3#_: As one seal—implies even for things where one seal suffices one letter counts as a sign and is better than a lock, as the Mechaber wrote in the next seif—Shach.
baer-heitev.4#א: Lock—see what is written above, s.k. 5.
baer-heitev.4#ב: The sack—meaning he sealed the sack as well.
baer-heitev.5#א: Kosher—Taz wrote: implies specifically b'dieved, but l'chatchila not.
baer-heitev.5#ב: And the like—Taz wrote: it seems obvious this includes a chicken in which nikkur of the neck tendons is recognizable as Israelites do, on which one may rely.
baer-heitev.5#ג: D'rabbanan—explained in Torat HaBayit: for a d'rabbanan prohibition, even if a Jew saw the seal was completely broken and it was clearly evident the seal was opened—it is permitted in this matter—Shach.
baer-heitev.6#_: Slaughtered—Shach wrote: and it is difficult regarding what is said in seif 1 that if his kids were lost, permitted if slaughtered—for there it was never in a non-Jew's hand, only we did not know who slaughtered, therefore we follow the majority that most found at slaughter are experts; but here, sending in a non-Jew's hand, there is concern he switched good for bad, therefore even where most Israelites are found we concern he slaughtered himself for the one he switched; Mordekhai wrote: an incident came—a slaughtered chicken sent via a non-Jew without a guard, they doubted perhaps another was switched, they asked the slaughterer if he slaughtered this chicken; he answered: I have no visual recognition in it; however now I slaughtered one chicken; but the owner recognized it and said this is it, and I permitted it since the owner recognized it, end of his words; Maharshal added: but if they did not ask the slaughterer it is not a sign—and it is simple (and see siman 63 what the Taz wrote there).
baer-heitev.7#_: To the public—Shach wrote: implies even with other Kutim who are not his slave and maidservant, permitted b'dieved in a public place (unlike Or Zarua who permitted only his slave and maidservant); and Taz wrote: even where Jews are not commonly found but only non-Jews—this non-Jew fears lest other non-Jews see him and tell the Israelite, as siman 129, seif 4; and in Torat Chatas he wrote the custom is to send via a non-Jew in a public thoroughfare that is an Israelite neighborhood where non-Jews are not found, end of his words.
baer-heitev.8#_: To switch—in siman 119 it will be explained: specifically for that thing he is suspect about, he is also suspect to switch—see there, Shach.
baer-heitev.9#א: Known—Taz wrote: I wonder greatly—perhaps it was truly an Israelite's and he made a sign to recognize it among treifah pieces, and afterward learned this was treifah, and therefore it is now in a non-Jew's hand—whence to be lenient in a d'oraisa doubt (and Nachalat Shiva answered: it deals where there is a seal or "kosher" written, which is not customary until known with certainty kosher—see there).
baer-heitev.9#ב: And b'dieved—Shach wrote: meaning if he already bought from the non-Jew (see Peri Chadash, s.k. 31); and it seems it deals where there is no concern stamps remained with non-Jews, etc.; but if there is concern stamps remained with non-Jews, forbidden even b'dieved; however the Levush wrote in great loss one may permit even then b'dieved; and Bach wrote the custom is to buy wines non-Jews bring from the land called Muscovy via their seals, for they bring writings from Israel—see siman 130, seif 6.
baer-heitev.10#א: And enters—Shach wrote: it seems even a child going out and entering helps, as above siman 115, seif 1, in the hagahah (and even for a d'oraisa prohibition); and the Gemara concludes even l'chatchila permitted with going out and entering—therefore what the Tur wrote "one who leaves" is because of the end: he stayed long and did not inform he intends to stay, which is permitted only b'dieved—see siman 129, seif 1.
baer-heitev.10#ב: Locked—and from presumption we say he did not lock unless it became known it was locked—Shach.
baer-heitev.11#א: To concern—and Peri Chadash wrote the view of most poskim is to permit even with going out and entering, and so is primary—see there; and from the Rosh's responsum it is proven even with non-Jew and Israelite guests we are not concerned, for what we permit with going out and entering is even with guests who do not know each other, for they also fear each other—see there, Shach.
baer-heitev.11#ב: To be careful—Shach wrote: meaning because of sparks; and since he wrote "even," when mouths are not open one need not be careful with two pots; and the Taz wrote the reason is lest they switch one for the other—accordingly, if two Israelite pots, one meat and one milk, no prohibition even l'chatchila to cook in one oven, since switching does not apply.
baer-heitev.12#א: And enters—Shach wrote: the Rav's view seems that with going out and entering one need not be stringent (the main stringency is when going to synagogue, where maidservants know they stay a while; but with actual going out and entering one need not be stringent at all—Shach and Peri Chadash); and from the previous seif that l'chatchila one should be careful even with two pots, it is simple that Israelite and non-Jew who set pots is no worse than going out and entering, for there the reason is sparks flying, as written above.
baer-heitev.12#ב: To feed her—in Shibolei HaLeket: not to that non-Jew nor other non-Jews—meaning she knew that thing was forbidden to an Israelite and nevertheless gave it; and he also wrote: a non-Jew who said do not eat from this pot, for I threw milk in it—we do not accept from him, rather it is permitted, end of his words; and so Torat Chatas: a non-Jew is not believed neither for prohibition nor permission—see siman 122, seif 3, and siman 127; and Mordekhai wrote: when an Israelite gives a non-Jew a cooked dish in a pot to bring to the non-Jew's house, the Israelite should warn him not to wash the bowl but leave some food residue, and likewise bring it back the same day, end of his words. One may wonder how he relies on telling the non-Jew to leave residue—perhaps he will use it and then return and put residue in it. Bach cited a responsum of Maharar Menachem of Cordova left among non-Jews: an Israelite had taken a little fat from the pot with a spoon, and when the pot returned with the fat he recognized the depression in the fat from which fat was taken—it seems to permit, for in such a case visual recognition applies, end of Taz.
baer-heitev.13#א: Perhaps—Shach wrote: since there are many doubts, it seems permitted to buy other cheeses from him—see there; and likewise we are not concerned he smeared, etc., for we are not concerned he intended to cause stumbling as long as the non-Jew has no benefit in the matter, as in this seif.
baer-heitev.13#ב: Resting—meaning he left it in a special place on the cheeses; but if he left it elsewhere, even intentionally in a special place, since he did not leave it resting on the cheeses the non-Jew thinks the Israelite does not know where he left it—and forbidden (but if left resting on the cheeses, then the non-Jew fears to take the stamp lest the Israelite made a sign in how he placed it)—Shach.

beer-hagolah.1#_: A statement of Rav, Avodah Zarah folio 39, and as the Tur wrote in the name of the Rashba: because it is a Torah prohibition; and so from the words of the Rambam, chapter 13 of the Mishneh Torah, law 10.
beer-hagolah.2#_: The language of the Rambam there (and R' Yerucham).
beer-hagolah.3#_: There; and even though stam yeinam is only d'rabbanan, they were stringent with it like Torah law because of the affection of libation upon them, and they trouble themselves and forge—Beit Yosef in the name of the Rashba.
beer-hagolah.4#_: Tur in Beit Yosef, and it is from the words of Tosafot, Avodah Zarah folio 31.
beer-hagolah.5#_: The Rosh there, from the words of Tosafot; and so agreed the Rosh and the Ran; and see further the law of wine agency below in siman 130.
beer-hagolah.6#_: Tur; and so the Rashba in Torat HaBayit, from the baraita of one who sends a barrel of wine, etc., folio 31, and as Tosafot explain there.
beer-hagolah.7#_: Tur; and so the Rashba in Torat HaBayit and the Ran in chapter 2 of Avodah Zarah in the name of R' Yitzchak.
beer-hagolah.8#_: The Rashba in responsum, Avodah Zarah, siman 130.
beer-hagolah.9#_: In Sefer HaChinuch in the name of the Ra'ah.
beer-hagolah.10#_: From the baraita: one who buys and one who rents, etc., and like R' Eliezer and like the Rashba's text that is lenient and makes a lock and seal like two seals, there folio 31.
beer-hagolah.11#_: Tur in the name of Rashi.
beer-hagolah.12#_: Tur in the name of the Rashba in Torat HaBayit and the Mordekhai in the end of Chullin in the name of Rashi.
beer-hagolah.13#_: There too in his name, from the variant of Rav Yirmiyah among the winepresses—Avodah Zarah folio 31.

beur-hagra.1#א: Deposited or, etc.—sent: 39b, two; and as Rashi explains there, forbidden, etc., with a seal, etc.; deposited: 31a, one; and as R' Yochanan holds, and so Rava explains there, seal within seal—clearly he holds so; and so holds there 39b, two; and so Rav Ashi, 29b, two, regarding cooked wine and vinegar; and Rav himself, 31a, one, ruled like R' Eliezer; and there 69b, two, halachah like R' Eliezer, etc.; Rabbenu Tam explained there 39b, two deals with a suspect Israelite who is worse than a non-Jew trusted to be believed; and so Rava and Rav Ashi—and thereby the case of Rav Bibi cutting three, etc., is resolved even though it is only one sign; and R' Yochanan explains there and there with a non-Jew: one seal suffices for a depositor who returns and sees his seal, for the non-Jew fears—in such a case dispute of R' Eliezer and the Rabbis, halachah like R' Eliezer; or a sender who informs through his writing about his seal and the non-Jew knows, he fears—then Rav Bibi's cutting, whose cut was known, as Rashi there, is resolved; but a sender who does not inform requires two seals. Rashba and Ran answered that even R' Eliezer requires seal within seal; they dispute only that for R' Eliezer lock and seal suffice, for the Rabbis specifically two seals, text 'his lock and seal'—and so Rif, Rosh, and Shulchan Piskei; and Tosafot there, both of them, halachah like R' Eliezer; they said one seal means with a lock—and so from Rif who ruled like R' Eliezer and said how seal within seal, etc.—and this is what 'deposited or sent' means per the Ran, and so I have explained, unlike R' Yochanan's view. In non-Jews' hands—to exclude Rabbenu Tam's view. (Likkut) Wine, etc., deposited or sent, etc.—Rashba and Tur in his name, unlike Rabbenu Tam and R' Yochanan (end of citation).
beur-hagra.1#ב: But wine, etc.—all this is the Rambam's language; cooked there 29b. (Likkut) But cooked wine, etc., and everything whose prohibition is d'rabbanan, etc.—Rambam's language; and so Rashba; Tur in the name of Rashba; Ran explained another reason; Tosafot there, he said, Taz (end of citation).
beur-hagra.1#ג: Or wine, etc.—as in Yerushalmi: confections have no stam yeinam; Rambam explained wine mixed with honey—and the same as cooked wine, and certainly beer; and dealt with in siman 123, seif 4.
beur-hagra.1#ה: And everything whose prohibition, etc.—as explained: chavivta with seal within seal because they are d'oraisa; but chamfig only rabbinically—Ba'er Heitev. (Likkut) Yerushalmi explains the reason: every matter whose prohibition is intrinsic—seal within seal because of mixture; one seal—apparently the Rambam explains because of rabbinic mixture prohibition; proof: bread whose prohibition is intrinsic—and Or Zarua; but Ra'ah wrote like the Yerushalmi's reason; now the text is fine—they deleted Rashi's 'bread—for what do we concern,' etc.; Tosafot there, bread, etc.; but accordingly it is resolved because its prohibition is intrinsic—except there 29b, also vinegar and cooked wine whose prohibition is intrinsic, he also said thus, that he does not trouble and forge with one seal; only for stam yeinam because of affection of libation requires seal within seal; therefore it must be as the Rambam: because it is rabbinic—and so the Ran (end of citation).
beur-hagra.1#ו: Deposited—and the same for sent, following the Rambam's language.
beur-hagra.1#ז: And some say, etc., and even, etc.—R' Yochanan's view; and in siman 130 he states the first view without a disputant. (Likkut) And some say, etc., and even, etc.—as R' Yochanan explains to resolve Rav against Rav and other difficulties of R' Eliezer who permits with one seal specifically for a depositor who will see his seal, etc.; and we say there: two, the sender of a barrel, etc.; Rashi on the barrel, etc.; and all the more via a non-Jew—clearly like R' Eliezer, yet recognition of the seal is needed because it is one seal and the recipient knows—one seal suffices even for a sender; but for seal within seal no seal recognition is needed; and per Rabbenu Tam who establishes the baraita of 'the recipient knows' like the Rabbis, nevertheless from rabbinic law we learn for R' Eliezer as Tosafot wrote—see there 69b, nevertheless, etc.; but Rabbenu Tam explains for R' Eliezer no seal recognition is needed at all, per his view establishing the baraita of knowing like the Rabbis and not deriving for R' Eliezer, because for R' Eliezer we are not concerned for forgery at all, as in the Gemara 69b, and per his view resolving the difficulties not regarding sender and depositor but distinguishing suspect Israelite and non-Jew—and this is the hagahah 'and some say,' etc.; but he also explains the baraita of knowing is not because of one seal but because he returned to his seal and found it damaged; but in ordinary cases no seal recognition is needed, no distinction between one seal and seal within seal, neither for R' Eliezer nor the Rabbis, even seal within seal—and this is seif 2 'once,' etc., and siman 130 seif 8 'sealed,' etc., and Tosafot there and there (end of citation).
beur-hagra.1#ח: And some say, etc.—Rabbenu Tam's view. (Likkut) And some say, not, etc.—Tosafot Bava Metzia 23b, three, etc., and Rosh there 63, and Rabbenu Tam, etc.—otherwise Rav against Rav is difficult; but in the first answer he explained the case of three horns is extra (end of citation).
beur-hagra.1#ט: And b'dieved, etc.—Tosafot there 2b, the sender, etc., and b'dieved, etc.—meaning even if he did not send to inform, as below regarding no recognition needed, even R' Yochanan agrees.
beur-hagra.2#א: Once, etc., but, etc.—there 31b, two, the sender of the house, etc.; Tosafot explain: if he returned to his seal, etc.; but l'chatchila need not see, as 69b, halachah, etc., we are not concerned for forgery—apparently we are not concerned at all; and so for the Rabbis with seal within seal, R' Eliezer is not invoked except they require only one seal; Tosafot there, why, etc., however since here in our sugya, etc., and the baraita above, etc., and there 31b, the sender; some are lenient to send, etc.; and per R' Yochanan, even though he must inform, nevertheless need not see, as Tosafot 69b, nevertheless; however if sending written Torah and informed his fellow, etc.—unlike the Ran who wrote per R' Yochanan's view specifically when the recipient knows; and Bahag deals there—see there.
beur-hagra.2#ב: However, etc.—from what is said 34b, for what do we concern ourselves, etc.; and in chapter 3 (95a), ten shops are brought, etc., found in a non-Jew's hand; Tosafot 12a, and he throws, etc.
beur-hagra.2#ג: Or, etc.—there 29b: if because of libation, etc., and if, etc.
beur-hagra.2#ד: Even, etc.—for even without any seal it would be permitted if not for concern of switching.
beur-hagra.4#א: Lock, etc.—like R' Eliezer and as the Rashba explained above.
beur-hagra.4#ב: But, etc.—certainly a lock is not a seal even for R' Eliezer—for therefore R' Eliezer was not asked about two locks; the Rabbis are explained only because since there is one seal he does not trouble to open with a lock—Chullin there; and end of chapter 17 of Shabbat: for R' Eliezer one seal suffices, clearly a lock is not a seal—and this is 69b: for R' Eliezer we are not concerned for forgery.
beur-hagra.4#ג: If one sends, etc., and if, etc.—meaning even without turning the stitches, the sack's stitching is like a lock unless turned—then it is a seal—and understand.
beur-hagra.5#א: If sent, etc.—Rashi in chapter 3, 94a, from that we say there 'Israel's cut,' etc.
beur-hagra.5#ב: And likewise all, etc.—the Rosh there from the above.
beur-hagra.5#ג: And specifically, etc.—Or Zarua in the name of Terumat HaDeshen.
beur-hagra.6#_: Sent, etc.—slaughter is not a sign, for Israelite is proven from the challenge in Bava Metzia 24b that they permitted it to him because of slaughter—majority are Israelites [Noda Biyehudah there and as I wrote siman 1, seif 4]; and Hagahot Asheri, first chapter of Chullin, siman 17, and he wrote, etc.
beur-hagra.7#_: If sent, etc.—Ba'al HaGadol; and in Tosefta, chapter 3 of Demai: sending via a non-Jew—concerned for tithes and shevi'it; but gentiles' grain measured from threshing floor to city—no concern for tithes or shevi'it because they are presumed guarded.
beur-hagra.8#א: One who buys, etc.—Ba'al HaGadol; Tosefta there: sending via a non-Jew or a Kuti—no concern for tithes or shevi'it.
beur-hagra.8#ב: And even, etc.—for even for slaughter they are believed, as in the eighth chapter of Zevachim; Tosafot Pesachim 4b, they believed him, etc.
beur-hagra.8#ג: And some, etc.—Avodah Zarah 39b; as Rabbenu Tam explained: with a suspect Israelite it deals, as above; specifically an am ha'aretz suspect regarding demai, a matter the public are lenient about, is believed; the Rambam per his view explaining there with a non-Jew, as above.
beur-hagra.9#א: Meat found, etc.—as in chapter 3: Israel's cut, etc.; we concern lest an Israelite buy—apparently permitted to buy, for we do not make an enactment for the wicked.
beur-hagra.9#ב: And that, etc.—as above, seif 66, regarding slaughter.
beur-hagra.9#ד: And some forbid, etc.—because we do not find such in the Gemara, and the Rashba's words above were omitted.
beur-hagra.10#_: (Likkut) If he, etc.—going out and entering is permitted in every case, even a Kuti who slaughters his animal and is occupied with it and can trample—even more so permitted, as at the beginning of Chullin; R' Nissim and Ra'avad, chapter 5 of Avodah Zarah (end of citation).
beur-hagra.11#א: (Likkut) Israelite, etc.—even though we say twelve months we do not say perhaps he turns back, etc.—it implies but if he turns back forbidden; Tosafot already explained there, perhaps—specifically with guests, and Rava disputes even in such a case (end of citation). (Likkut) Israelite, etc.—Ba'al HaGadol; see there at length in R' Nissim and he concludes: from everyone's words we learn Israelite, etc.—not because of nevelah nor because of pipe, etc.—see there (end of citation).
beur-hagra.11#ב: Perhaps when he turned, etc.—Tur's language, unlike Mordekhai and Hagahot Asheri.
beur-hagra.11#ג: Even if, etc.—Tosafot there, and as explained. (Likkut) Even if, etc.—Tosafot there, and he throws, etc.; in such a case Abaye is concerned but Rava disputes him; and Rashi on Rava, etc., must read 'he fears' and 'he fears'—two reasons; and even with superior meat, as we hold everywhere going out and entering is permitted, like Tosafot's question above and as in this seif 'if he,' etc., unlike Hagahot Asheri there, it implies, etc.—and this is what the Rosh wrote there: on this we rely, etc., and also it is, etc.—for Rava permits, and even for Tosafot's first answer behold Rava disputes him (end of citation).
beur-hagra.11#ד: And even their mouths, etc., and we are not, etc.—there.
beur-hagra.11#ה: And the same, etc.—chapter Keitzad Tzolin (76b): nevelah meat, etc., and roasted—as in siman 108.
beur-hagra.11#ו: But l'chatchila, etc.—not only roasting because of smell, as siman 108; but even in a pot because of sparks; and otherwise forbidden because of mixture, as there—except what does 'however,' etc., mean—e.g., they roasted in two pots.
beur-hagra.12#_: One should be stringent, etc.—as in this seif: without going out and entering forbidden if he benefits; and here too sometimes she puts milk in the pot to improve her portion; and when going to synagogue, as the Rosh wrote. (Likkut) One should be stringent, etc.—there in the Rosh: and for God-fearing, etc.—meaning when going to synagogue, for it is not actual going out and entering, for it is like informing he intends to stay—which is forbidden as in this seif; and even though we say seventy elders heard the sound of roasting and it is permitted—for he informs his donkey-driver there the non-Jew knows the Israelite is careful about him—and this is 'he informs his driver,' unlike here; and it is permitted only from the second reason that he does not benefit—and on this he said 'and also to improve her portion,' etc.; and this is the hagahah 'and he does not go out and enter'—for with going out and entering even l'chatchila permitted as at the beginning of Chullin (end of citation). (Likkut) One should be stringent, etc.—for the Rosh wrote there: on this we rely, etc., when going to synagogue—and apparently proof for the Rabbis from what is written: 38a, one, 'one who leaves,' etc., sets, etc.; but in the Yerushalmi they said on it: when the child sits and guards (end of citation).
beur-hagra.13#א: Israelite, etc.—Pri Chadash, s.k. 40; and in Hagahot Maimoniyot in the name of Rivba: for the reason of siman 115, seif 3 (in s.k. 18) in the name of the Rashba—one should not permit as I wrote siman 115, seif 3. (Likkut) Israelite, etc.—see there in the Mordekhai: R' Yitzchak permitted because he holds that otherwise there is no reason to forbid cheeses nowadays because of the reason of exposure (main); and as Tosafot there (35a, one, etc.); and also in Hagahot Maimoniyot there: because we hold taste like substance is d'rabbanan like Rashi, and one may be lenient in its doubt; except he wrote even for Rabbenu Tam who holds taste like substance is d'oraisa one may be lenient because there are many doubts—perhaps the stamp never came to the non-Jew's hand; and if it came, perhaps he did not forge; and if he forged, perhaps he only stamped with something permitted—for the same reason we permit ordinary gentile vessels because of many doubts (end of citation).
beur-hagra.13#ב: And likewise we are not, etc.—as above, he has no benefit.
beur-hagra.13#ג: But if he did not, etc.—even in a special place—and Pri Chadash.

kaf-hachayim.1#_: A) [Seif 1] Wine and meat, etc.—in the Gemara, Avodah Zarah 39, tekhelet also requires two seals; in Shulchan Aruch it was omitted because tekhelet is not found in our time, as in Midrash Tanchuma, parashat Shelach; and so Minchat Yaakov (klal 32, letter 22). It is known that in the generation before ours the Gaon R' Gershon Henoch of Radzin produced the chilazon from which tekhelet is dyed, and the great ones of his generation disputed him, including the Gaon of Koenigsberg in Yeshuot Malki (Orach Chaim, siman 2), and he hinted briefly in Arukh HaShulchan Orach Chaim (siman 9, letter 12); see responsum Basheilim Rosh (siman 244); and see in Sefer Shulchan Melachim (Darkei Yosef 1a); and understand.
kaf-hachayim.2#_: B) And meat—even with majority of Israelite slaughterers we require seal within seal for meat, since the Mechaber ruled (siman 63) that meat lost from sight is forbidden—Shach s.k. 1, Peri Chadash s.k. 1, Lechem HaPanim s.k. 1, Erekh Shai. However, at first glance it is not so from the Rashba (siman 466) who wrote—and know in a city of Israelite slaughterers and majority of sellers selling slaughtered meat and also nevelah meat found there in a non-Jew's hand is permitted; nevertheless it seems one does not send l'chatchila meat via a non-Jew without a seal, etc., even though b'dieved one may permit when found in a non-Jew's hand, end of his words—brought in Bedek HaBayit; and so noted in Sefer Chadarim Da'ah. One may say the Rashba follows his view disputing the Rambam and permitting when found in a non-Jew's hand like our Gemara (Chullin 95)—unlike the Mechaber who ruled like the Rambam that even then forbidden, therefore we require seal within seal; but in Knesset Yehudah he wrote to reject the Peri Chadash—for since from the Torah we follow the majority and the prohibition is only d'rabbanan, one seal suffices; therefore he established the Mechaber's words only where there is no majority of Israelite slaughterers—see there; and so Yeshuot Yaakov s.k. 2; and so in Minchat Chinuch (klal 32, s.k. 52); and so from the Perishah, letter 11—see there; and see in Shach below s.k. 25.
kaf-hachayim.3#_: C) And a piece of fish—specifically a piece of fish; for a whole fish or half fish would be recognizable by fin and scale, as above siman 83—Perishah letter 1, Shach s.k. 2, Kenesset HaGadol hagahah letter 1, Lechem HaPanim s.k. 2.
kaf-hachayim.4#_: D) Deposited or sent via a non-Jew—even l'chatchila permitted to deposit or send via a non-Jew Torah prohibitions with seal within seal and rabbinic prohibitions with one seal, as the Mechaber wrote explicitly (end of siman 130)—Shach s.k. 3, Kenesset HaGadol hagahah s.k. 3, Peri Chadash s.k. 3, Lechem HaPanim s.k. 1; and so agreed in Zivchei Tzedek s.k. 1. He rejected Knesset Yehudah who wrote per the Mechaber's view only b'dieved—see there.
kaf-hachayim.5#א: E) Via a non-Jew—and it seems this means specifically an idol-worshipping gentile; but Ishmaelites who are not idol worshippers—permitted to send via them or deposit with them wine with one seal, for the Mechaber rules like the Rif, Rambam, and Rashba that Torah prohibitions need seal within seal and rabbinic ones one seal; the Rashba wrote: even though stam yeinam is only d'rabbanan, they were stringent like Torah because of affection of libation—they trouble and forge one seal, end of his words; therefore with Ishmaelites, where affection of libation does not apply, one seal suffices. Even if one says perhaps he bought from another idol-worshipping gentile who libated—in Ishmaelite wine too one could say so, yet we are not concerned to forbid benefit, as below (siman 124, seif 6); see Kenesset HaGadol (there, Hagahat Beit Yosef letter 19); see Avodah Zarah (64) and below (siman 128); therefore the same here; and so from most Acharonim brought below s.k. 26.
kaf-hachayim.5#ב: E) And greater: we find the Taz, s.k. 4, wrote that in our time there is no affection of libation and wine suffices with one seal—see there; and Minchat Yaakov (klal 32, letter 32) agreed; and in his responsa Shevut Yaakov, part 1 (siman 63); and the conditions of those who support them: Or Zarua (chapter 2 of Avodah Zarah, siman 160) and Rokeach (siman 496) wrote that in our time, when gentiles do not libate to idolatry, one need not seal within seal, as we say regarding vinegar, etc.—see there; and so the Meiri (Avodah Zarah 31), regarding one who deposited his wine, in the name of some later rabbis who permitted wine even for drinking via one seal, because in these days libation is not common to them as in those times, end of his words (the publishing rabbi, letter 3, did not mention the above); see Arukh HaShulchan s.k. 13 that one should rule like the Taz; and it is true all this does not suffice for the Mechaber's view that we accepted his rulings that wine needs seal within seal (and it seems per his reason he forbids stam yeinam in our time even for benefit in siman 123—unlike dissenters); and so explicitly in responsum Chakrei Lev, part 1, Yoreh Deah (siman 199): from the poskim who ruled even in our time two seals for wine; and again brought the Rashba in Torat HaBayit (141a): even though gentiles today are not idol worshippers, nevertheless since some among them libate, we require seal within seal; Beit Yosef brought it (siman 128) and concluded even b'dieved forbidden; and so the Rama's hagahah there; he concluded: nevertheless to permit in great loss one may rely on this great authority—see there; and see responsum Yismach Lev, Gagin (Yoreh Deah, siman 8); in Yeshuot Yaakov s.k. 4 he wrote explicitly unlike the Taz; and so in Sefer Erekh Shai—see there; nevertheless with Ishmaelites it seems there is less concern; and I do not deny I saw in Or Sameach (1 Kings 5:32) he explained the Rambam there to forbid drinking when he transgressed and deposited with an Ishmaelite with one seal—see there; but in my opinion one may rely and be lenient on all the above; however l'chatchila one should heed Or Sameach to require two seals even with Ishmaelites; see Lechem Mishneh (1 Kings 5:32); see responsum Tashbetz, part 3 (siman 89); responsum Bnei Binyamin (siman 6); Sefer Ginzei Chaim (maarechet 8, end of letter 91)—and understand.
kaf-hachayim.6#_: F) Via a non-Jew—and the same with a suspect Israelite, as below seif 8; he mentioned non-Jew because of wine—for the reason for wine is affection of libation, he troubles and forges; unlike a suspect Israelite where one seal suffices like other rabbinic prohibitions—Shach s.k. 4, Lechem HaPanim s.k. 3, Zivchei Tzedek s.k. 3; and the Gaon Beit Meir agreed with the Shach regarding wine for a suspect Israelite that one seal suffices; he wrote what Tosafot (Avodah Zarah 31) wrote in the name of Rabbenu Tam that for a suspect Israelite seal within seal is needed—this means an Israelite suspect to libate—see there (and see Bach who also addressed Tosafot's view—see there); unlike Knesset Yehudah who wrote that even for a suspect Israelite we concern gentiles will ask him because of their affection of libation—see there; the main point is like the other Acharonim; and so responsum Radbaz, part 3 (siman 528); see Pri Toar s.k. 26; and what is written below s.k. 40; and mainly the law of a suspect Israelite—see below s.k. 83 and siman 119, s.k. 14.
kaf-hachayim.7#_: G) But cooked wine—in Beit Yosef below (siman 123) he brought the Rashba in Torat HaBayit: what is cooked? Whatever was boiled is cooked, and so received from the Geonim; some say it is not called cooked until its measure diminishes through cooking; it seems impossible to boil without diminishing measure, and the Geonim's reception decides, end of his words; and so the Ran; also the Rosh agreed with the Ra'avad in the name of the Geonim that if boiled it is certainly cooked; and so in Sefer HaTerumah; and so the Tur ruled there: from when is it called cooked—from when it boiled on the fire; the Shach wrote there s.k. 7 that this means its measure diminishes through boiling, end of his words; and so ruled Or Zarua (chapter 2 of Avodah Zarah, siman 215); responsum Tashbetz, part 1 (siman 29); Orchot Chaim Yoreh Deah (page 247); and more; the Geonim's words in Sha'arei Teshuvah (siman 258)—see there. However, Kenesset HaGadol (siman 123, Hagahat Beit Yosef letter 14) wrote in the name of the Riaz: the measure of cooked wine is whatever is not drunk as wine [and see Kenesset HaGadol there letter 50 regarding vinegar]. However, Shulchan Gavoah (there s.k. 7) wrote the Riaz's view is nullified against all these rabbis who hold whatever was boiled on the fire, however much, is considered cooked; brought to law in Sefer Einei David (chapter 6, page 3) and Zikhronenu LeChaim, part 2 (folio 31b)—see there. We find the Rambam (chapter 6 of Issurei Mizbeach, law 9): cooked on fire until its taste changed through cooking (unfit for libation); therefore it is proven that even for stam yeinam prohibition we require cooking until taste changes; as written (chapter 1 of Mishneh Torah, law 9)—see there; and so proved in Mishor Ba'ahalei Teshuvah (siman 123, s.k. 5) and R' Menuchah—see there; and so the Meiri (Avodah Zarah 29:) wrote: the end of the matter in this topic—in my opinion whatever is cooked until its taste changed from what it was, etc., its charm is nullified and there is no affection of libation on it, end of his words; the publishing rabbi noted the Rambam's words there—see there; and so for law in Sefer Kikar Le'aden (folio 162a) in the name of Maharam of Lunzano: what is written 'cooked wine has no stam yeinam' is not ordinary cooking but extensive cooking until taste changed in cooking—brought in Sefer Ikrei HaDat (siman 13, letter 13); and Maharach Palaggi in Ruach Chaim (siman 123, s.k. 2) explained the Riaz's view—that is also until taste changed from wine taste—see there; see Sefer Vayomer Yitzchak (folio 114b); we found accordingly companions to the Riaz, unlike Shulchan Gavoah that his view is nullified against all poskim and he did not mention the Rambam's view; and so the Meiri and R' Menuchah—as said; and so ruled Ben Ish Chai, part 2 (parashat Balak, letter 7); see Sefer Beit Aharon Krispin (folio 44b); responsum Shevitat Yom Tov (Yoreh Deah, siman 1-4); see Kisei Eliyahu (siman 123, s.k. 2)—and understand. For law, in my opinion l'chatchila one should heed the Rambam and his camp and require seal within seal as long as wine has not reached the measure that taste changed; but b'dieved one should not be stringent, since many poskim hold boiling alone suffices; and so is the Mechaber's view we accepted; therefore if there was only one seal one may be lenient.
kaf-hachayim.8#_: H) And beer—and even though beer of gentiles is permitted, one may say it deals with wanting to drink the beer deposited with the gentile in his house, as above siman 114 to forbid this—Beit Meir; or one may say it deals with beer made from raisin wine—Ma'aseh Rokeach, chapter 13 of Mishneh Torah, law 10, brought in Zivchei Tzedek s.k. 3; and it seems even if he deposited ordinary beer he needs one seal lest he switch it with beer made from raisin wine, unless raisin beer is more expensive—in such a case we are not concerned for switching, as we hold in Avodah Zarah (34) and Shulchan Aruch (siman 114, seif 11); and so in responsum Tiferet Adam in his memoirs (maarechet 10, letter 5)—see there; and one may concern he mixes white wine in it—see Beit Meir there; responsum Radbaz, part 4 (siman 239)—see there.
kaf-hachayim.9#_: I) Or wine into which other things were mixed, such as honey—and it deals with mixing so much honey that the wine's taste changed because of it—for then there is no stam yeinam, as we hold (siman 123, seif 4); Lechem HaPanim—since there is stam yeinam concern, seal within seal is needed—Shach s.k. 6, Kenesset HaGadol hagahah letter 8, Peri Chadash s.k. 6, Minchat Yaakov klal 32 letter 34, Lechem HaPanim s.k. 4, Mesgeret HaShulchan, Zivchei Tzedek s.k. 4; see responsum Amek HaMelech (siman 48). In my opinion, since the Rambam's and Western Geonim's view permits even a little honey, and R' Elazar bar Natan in responsum of the Rivash (siman 180), even though other poskim dispute them—in b'dieved and great loss one may permit with one seal, since the custom in Egypt is lenient like the Rambam and Western Geonim even l'chatchila, as Or Zarua, part 2 (chapter 7 of Avodah Zarah, siman 262) and Hagahot Asheri (there 30); and so the Mechaber in Beit Yosef in responsum Avkat Rocheil (simanim 67); he rejected with both hands the sage who wanted to be stringent for them—see there; and responsum Radbaz, part 3 (siman 527) permitted in pressed circumstances to rely on Western Geonim—except he wrote this regarding Ishmaelite contact—see there; and with the Taz and Minchat Yaakov's views brought above (s.k. 5) that in our time gentiles are not idol worshippers, one seal suffices—in b'dieved and great loss one may well rely on them with a little honey; this is the case—to be lenient in responsum Mabit (siman 208)—see there.
kaf-hachayim.10#_: J) And know: for cooked wine and wine with honey—some say we permit only when the gentile knows it is cooked or has honey, as Be'er HaGolah (siman 123, s.k. 4) in the name of two sons of David: only then there is no stam yeinam—see there; and so Zikhronenu LeChaim (folio 31b); therefore the same here—if the gentile does not know, one may not permit except seal within seal. However, in Egypt they practiced leniency in stam yeinam even without this; and poskim stated their words generally on this; in any case b'dieved one seal suffices even if the gentile does not know; and with the Taz and Minchat Yaakov as above; see responsum Shevut Yaakov (siman 63).
kaf-hachayim.11#_: K) And likewise vinegar—meaning vinegar of wine, bubbling when poured on the ground, then full vinegar unfit for libation, as we hold (siman 123, seif 6); therefore no concern for affection of libation since unfit for libation; if for switching—stam yeinam is only d'rabbanan, one seal suffices—Shach s.k. 7, Kenesset HaGadol hagahah letter 8, Peri Chadash s.k. 7, Lechem HaPanim s.k. 5, Minchat Yaakov klal 32 letter 34, Mesgeret HaShulchan, Zivchei Tzedek s.k. 5. In my opinion b'dieved there is room to be lenient with one seal even when it has not reached bubbling measure—since the Mechaber's main view stringency requiring this measure is not agreed by all poskim; as Beit Yosef in the name of the Rashba in Torat HaBayit: this is not from the essence of the Gemara; whatever was wine and soured, between beginning and end of souring is no more than three days, etc.—see there; see Ritva's commentary (Avodah Zarah 29:); responsum Shem Aryeh (Yoreh Deah, siman 29): this measure is from stringency and not law, since it is unfit for libation—see there; see Orach Chaim (siman 204, seif 4) and Acharonim there; see responsum Chesed LeAvraham Elkelai (Orach Chaim, siman 5)—if so, at least here there is no affection of libation; responsum Chatam Sofer (siman 124); and with poskim who hold to be lenient in our time with wine with one seal—it seems for vinegar one may be lenient b'dieved even without bubbling measure; see Kenesset HaGadol siman 123 hagahah letter 11.
kaf-hachayim.12#א: L) And milk—and even though gentile milk is forbidden lest he switch with impure milk, a Torah prohibition—nevertheless one seal suffices because impure milk is recognizable, as Avodah Zarah (35:) pure white, impure green; therefore no concern he switches all or most, only perhaps a little forbidden only d'rabbanan—for min b'mino nullified in majority d'oraisa—Perishah s.k. 4, Shach s.k. 8, Taz s.k. 1, Peri Chadash s.k. 5, Lechem Mishneh chapter 13 of Mishneh Torah law 10, Shulchan Gavoah s.k. 10, Arukh HaShulchan s.k. 2. But Noda Biyehudah Mahadura Tinyana (Orach Chaim, siman 66) challenged the Shach: taste differs between impure and pure milk—it would be not its species; even though the Prisha (siman 98, s.k. 4) wrote where similar in name but different in taste, if not a complete taste change but slight, it is min b'mino—who testified the difference between impure and pure milk is only slight? Therefore the Noda Biyehudah wrote: the Shach's reasoning is fine that d'oraisa nullified in majority even noten ta'am gamur, because we hold taste like substance d'oraisa only for negative commandments with lashes, but impure milk is only a positive commandment—we do not learn taste like substance from gentile utensils or sheretz; it is d'rabbanan, therefore one seal suffices, end of his words; and in the Meiri (Avodah Zarah 39:) he wrote similarly to the Shach; if he held like the Noda Biyehudah he would not state such a great novelty obscurely; and as the Meiri wrote in Ritva's commentary and Rashba in Torat HaBayit (house 3, gate 6) and Beit HaLevi (chapter 3 of Mishneh Torah, law 16)—see there; in Sefer Be'er Yaakov (folio 218b) he also challenged the Shach like the Noda Biyehudah: since we follow taste, impure and pure milk tastes are not the same, as the Shach wrote (siman 107) regarding impure and pure fish—that would be not its species—see there; not necessary—for there too we find the Gra'a and Beit Meir who wrote they are min b'mino; and I found a tannaitic support: the Meiri (Chullin 97:) wrote explicitly—see there; responsum Nefesh Chayah (simanim 24-25); one may say here too impure and pure milk tastes are the same; and so I saw the Gaon Beit Meir (this siman) agreed with the Shach that impure and pure milk tastes are the same, like impure and pure fish—see there; in any case one may say their tastes are close; and we come to the Prisha's view that in such a case they are min b'mino; also the gentile may mix a little impure milk in pure so it will not be noticed in tasting; responsum Eiruvei HaBosem, part 2 (siman 117); Sefer Eiruvei HaBosem on Yoreh Deah (siman 81, s.k. 4); responsum Shem Aryeh (siman 52)—see there.
kaf-hachayim.12#ב: L) And one must see well in responsum Tashbetz, part 3 (siman 143): milk a gentile milked and a Jew was present—doubt d'oraisa because of impure milk mixture, and perhaps he mixed much—see there; and so Mar bar Rav in responsum of the Rashbash (siman 555)—we learn two things from them: A) it would be not its species and therefore Torah prohibition—unlike the Shach and camp; B) taste like substance d'oraisa even for positive commandments like impure milk—unlike the Noda Biyehudah. I found in responsum Maharsham, part 2 (siman 42): asked on Or Zarua (klal 31, law 14): impure milk that fell in a pot would be a doubt, implying unlike the Noda Biyehudah who holds his taste is d'rabbanan; he answered Or Zarua holds like Tosafot Bekhorot (6:), whom the Peri Megadim brought (siman 81)—impure milk is d'oraisa and lashes apply, disputing the Rambam that there are no lashes—see there. In my opinion it is strained to say so of the Rashbetz and Rashbash—for presumably they hold like the Rambam that it is a positive commandment; especially since the Mabit also wrote in Kiryat Sefer (chapter 3 of Mishneh Torah) it would be a doubt—see there; see Be'er HaGolah (siman 105, s.k. 1) who brought the Rashbetz's view [there is a textual error in his citation] and challenged: if so why does one seal suffice for milk? Be'er HaGolah answered siman this s.k. 2: perhaps he holds like Bach that the reason is he has no profit from switching, therefore they were not concerned even though d'oraisa—see there; see Kenesset HaGadol Hagahat Beit Yosef letter 12; nevertheless for those Tosafot (Bekhorot 6:) otherwise— they hold like Tosafot (Avodah Zarah 39:) that the reason is chamfig has no prohibition intrinsically except through mixture—see there.
kaf-hachayim.12#ג: L) At first glance I would attribute this to the dispute among Acharonim whether for prohibition coming from half measure we say taste like substance d'oraisa—Chochmat Adam (siman 105, s.k. 5) holds taste like substance d'oraisa only for full measure, unlike half measure; if so, the same for impure milk without lashes—it would be like chatzi shiur where we do not say taste like substance; and so the Rambam (chapter 3 of Mishneh Torah, law 6): milk of impure animal and eggs of impure bird are forbidden d'oraisa without lashes—'one who eats them is like eating chatzi shiur,' see there; unlike those who dispute Chochmat Adam—this too would be chatzi shiur taste d'oraisa; but one may say unlike chatzi shiur, for this comes from a prohibition that has lashes at full measure, unlike here where lashes do not apply to it; I found in responsum Avnei Nezer, Orach Chaim, part 2 (siman 259) who challenged the Noda Biyehudah: this is like chatzi shiur as the Rambam wrote; and since chatzi shiur taste is d'oraisa as proven in Chullin (98)—so too impure milk—see there; not necessary—one may say as written; and so explicitly responsum Shem Aryeh (Yoreh Deah, siman 52); but neither addressed Chochmat Adam; even for chatzi shiur one may say it is d'rabbanan; in Darkei Teshuvah (siman 98, s.k. 32) he brought also Knesset HaPanim holds like Chochmat Adam; nevertheless for milk mixture they challenged in Avnei Nezer and Shem Aryeh: here it is different—taste and substance; no need to learn from sheretz and gentile utensils since there is an olive's bulk in any case—see there.
kaf-hachayim.12#ד: L) And behold, even though in responsum Avnei Nezer (Orach Chaim, siman 259) he rejected the Noda Biyehudah with both hands and wrote the matter is clear to all poskim that even here taste like substance d'oraisa, and the Noda Biyehudah alone was lenient—see there—nevertheless several Acharonim tread in the Noda Biyehudah's hem; even Shem Aryeh does not dispute him for law; as he himself wrote in Sefer Eiruvei HaBosem Yoreh Deah (siman 92, s.k. 5) like the Noda Biyehudah; and so there (siman 107); responsum Yehudah Yaaleh Asad (Yoreh Deah, siman 130); Sefer Darkei Horaah, part 2 (chapter 71); responsum Levushei Mordekhai, part 1 (Yoreh Deah, siman 63); responsum Amudei Or (siman 51)—see there in conclusion he wrote he did not rely on this in practice; one may say; see responsum Pnei Meivin (Yoreh Deah, siman 103); responsum Sha'arei Rachamim Franki, part 2 (siman 5); however in responsum Be'er Yitzchak (Yoreh Deah, siman 13) he wrote to reject the Noda Biyehudah; also responsum Eiruvei HaBosem, part 2 (siman 117) left the Noda Biyehudah in doubt; there is room to rely on the Noda Biyehudah; responsum Maharsham, part 2 (siman 42) supported challenging the Noda Biyehudah; again established in Sefer Ein HaRo'im (folio 131a) who brought it to law; and so Mar bar Rav relied on it in his responsum (there, letter 71).
kaf-hachayim.12#ה: L) In Be'er HaGolah s.k. 2 he challenged the Shach on this per Rav's view (Avodah Zarah 39:) that milk suffices with one seal—for he holds min b'mino is not nullified d'oraisa; answer per above: since he has no profit he does not trouble and forge, as Bach—see there; and in Degel Machaneh Ephraim and Hagahot Ra'anan they addressed this—see there; see Yeshuot Yaakov s.k. 3; responsum Chatam Sofer (Yoreh Deah, siman 97); responsum Be'er Yitzchak (siman 13); Eiruvei HaBosem (siman 117) above; Sefer Devarim Aharon Polonski (siman 11)—and understand.
kaf-hachayim.13#_: M) And morayes—meaning where their custom is to put wine in it, therefore concern he switches with their morayes; if wine was dearer than morayes, or where they do not put wine in it—permitted to deposit with a non-Jew and send via him without any seal, as Shulchan Aruch above (siman 114, seif 11); and so Shach s.k. 9 and other Acharonim.

mateh-yehonatan.1#_: (Siman 118 in Shulchan Aruch, seif 4) But for things where one seal suffices, etc.—the lock is not counted as a seal. And see Shach, s.k. 22; and what he wrote: even though for Rabbenu Tam certainly a lock alone suffices, nevertheless we do not rely on him except with one seal—and the Shach's words seem puzzling, for since the Rama ruled there like Rabbenu Tam that with a non-Jew one seal suffices, why do we not rely also on a lock alone? It seems: even according to Rabbenu Tam who distinguishes between a suspect Israelite and a non-Jew—for with a non-Jew he holds like R' Eliezer that one seal suffices—nevertheless he does not hold entirely like R' Eliezer, for certainly for R' Eliezer who holds one seal suffices and makes no distinction at all between suspect and non-Jew—because he is not concerned for forgery at all—therefore there is no distinction between suspect Israelite and non-Jew, and therefore a lock also suffices; but for Rav who said seal within seal—because he is concerned for forgery—therefore there is room to distinguish between suspect Israelite and non-Jew: a non-Jew is permitted with one seal because he fears, and a suspect Israelite does not fear, as the poskim write in several places; therefore he needs two seals; and accordingly, even though R' Eliezer said lock or seal—for his view we are not concerned for forgery at all, so what difference between seal and lock; but for us who hold like Rav that we are concerned for forgery and distinguish between non-Jew and suspect Israelite because of fear—therefore even where a suspect Israelite is permitted with one seal, there is a difference between lock and seal: with a seal he fears since he sees an Israelite's seal and is seized as a thief, but with a lock one cannot say so—he does not fear, and we are concerned for forgery; therefore the Rama did not emend anything here—and the matter is clear to one who understands.
mateh-yehonatan.2#_: (Shach, s.k. 26) And the Mordekhai wrote in the chapter of Gid HaNashe, etc.—an incident came before me, etc.—and he added: but if they did not ask the slaughterer, it is not a sign, etc.—see there; meaning: even if there were no concern of switching at all, it should be forbidden because we are concerned perhaps the non-Jew did not want to go and trouble himself with the slaughterer and slaughtered it himself; but if the slaughterer says it was with him, we see he was not concerned about the trouble—therefore it is permitted; unlike without asking the slaughterer, which is forbidden as written—and understand well.
mateh-yehonatan.3#_: (There, Shulchan Aruch seif 9) And that non-Jews who know how to write are not found there. And even though above in seif 63 the Mechaber wrote this view in the name of "some say," implying not all agree; and here he states it without a disputant—it must be said: there it deals with depositing with a non-Jew, where we can say since he deposited with him and wrote letters on it, we say presumably this is what he deposited and we are not concerned he switched his and also went to a non-Jew who knows to write letters—two concerns, which we do not concern ourselves about; unlike here, meat found in a non-Jew's hand where there is only one concern—that perhaps he bought from a non-Jew who knows to write—and all agree we are concerned; understand well.
mateh-yehonatan.4#_: (There, Shulchan Aruch seif 10) And if he does not benefit from switching, permitted in every case, etc.—the Peri Chadash challenged: in Avodah Zarah 39b it is proven that even when he does not benefit from switching we are concerned for switching—for it says regarding bread: for what do we concern ourselves, etc.—if for switching, etc.—if they are equal, etc.—since there is one seal he does not trouble and forge; therefore it is proven that even where there is no benefit from switching one seal is needed; and the resolution is: certainly with bread, if he sent bread via a non-Jew, there is room to concern that perhaps he will have no bread for the non-Jew until he must use the Israelite's bread, and afterward when he wants to fulfill his agency he will switch with his own bread—if so, there is no greater benefit from switching, and we are concerned for switching; unlike where we know the non-Jew has his own bread—in such a case certainly we are not concerned for switching where he has no benefit from the Israelite.
mateh-yehonatan.5#_: (There, seif 11) An Israelite and a non-Jew who set two pots, etc.—permitted and we are not concerned, etc.—behold, if the Israelite certainly turned away, if we forbid the dish, Hagahot Asheri brings two views: it implies that if the Israelite turns away we are concerned; and from this the Rav Peter rules in the name of Rabbenu Tam that if two pots were on one stove, etc., and the Israelite turned away we are concerned lest the non-Jew throw nevelah and it is forbidden; and R' Margenstern permits, end of his words. Some want to prove that Tosafot also hold to forbid, for Tosafot challenged at the beginning of Avodah Zarah 13a: perhaps he turns back, etc.—and if so, even here permitted even if he turned away—then Tosafot's question is not difficult, for truly here too permitted like other prohibitions; therefore it must be they hold that if he turned away it is forbidden, and their answer seems to imply this: if he turned away forbidden—from their answer that here it deals where he is not seized as a thief; but in truth their words give no decisive ruling—certainly they hold permitted even if he turns away; rather their question is: the reason we are not concerned, etc., should be taught that it has the law of going out and coming in—for this Tosafot answered that going out and coming in does not help here because he is not seized as a thief; therefore they had to say we are not concerned when he turns away—and understand well.

mechaber.1#main: The law of a piece of meat or a food item sent via a non-Jew. It contains 13 seifim: Wine, meat, and a piece of fish that has no distinguishing mark, that was deposited or sent in the hand of a non-Jew, requires two seals; but cooked wine and beer, or wine into which other things were mixed, such as honey, and likewise vinegar, milk, morayes, bread, and cheese, and everything whose prohibition is from the words of the scribes (d'rabbanan), that was deposited in the hand of a non-Jew—is permitted with one seal. And some say that even for things that require two seals, they said so only regarding sending via a non-Jew who is not going to see the seal; but for one who deposits it, who will see his seal, one seal suffices, for he will fear. And even the sender—if he informed his fellow the form of the seal, and also told the non-Jew that he informed his fellow—one seal suffices. {Rama: And some say that we do not require two seals except for a Jew who is suspect; but with a non-Jew, everything is permitted via one seal (Tur and poskim in the name of Rabbenu Tam). And b'dieved one may rely on this (Arukh, rule 23, and Hagahot Maimoniyot and Tosafot).}
mechaber.2#main: Once they sealed properly with two seals on things that need two and with one on things where one suffices, one need not go back afterward to inspect it; but if he went back to his seal and did not recognize it, it is forbidden—even if he made two seals (this seif is duplicated in siman 130, seif 8): {Rama: However, this is specifically if it is something where there is concern that it was switched and he benefits from the switch (Tur and Beit Yosef in the name of Tosafot and other poskim), or it is wine and there is concern that he forbade it through contact; but if one sees the thing that was sent or deposited and it is good as it was sent, and the non-Jew would not benefit if he switched it, we are not concerned—even if the seal is damaged. And see below at the end of siman 130 these laws.}
mechaber.3#main: One letter counts as one seal; two count as two seals. And stamps—even though they have several letters—are not counted except as one seal, since they affix them at one time. And some say that in a place where apostates and Kutim who know how to write are found, writing is not a sign except for one who recognizes the script (this seif is duplicated in siman 130, seif 6).
mechaber.4#main: A lock and seal count as two seals; but for things where one seal suffices, if it had only a lock, the lock is not counted as a seal (this too is duplicated there, seif 66): {Rama: If one sends something in a sack and seals the sack, it is not even like one seal (Kol Bo in the name of the Rif and Or Zarua and Tosefta, siman 130) unless he turned the stitches inward (Arukh); and if he sealed the thing he sent and also the sack, it counts as two seals (Kol Bo there).}
mechaber.5#main: If one sent via a non-Jew a thigh without a seal, if it is cut the way an Israelite cuts it after removal of the gid—it is kosher; and likewise any piece in which Israelite nikkur is recognizable, such as through removal of the foreleg tendon and the tendon near the breast, and the like: {Rama: And the other pieces with it—if there is concern about them that they were switched, they are forbidden (so ruled the Terumat HaDeshen, siman 200, in the name of R' Meshullam Ashiri, responsum 378); and this is specifically for meat or another d'oraisa prohibition; but if he sent a d'rabbanan prohibition, such as cheeses where there is concern that perhaps the non-Jew switched them—if he recognizes some of them that not all were switched, they are permitted if those that were not switched are the better ones that he sent, for certainly if he switched he would take the best among them (there).}
mechaber.6#main: If one sent via a non-Jew an animal or bird that were slaughtered without a seal, they are forbidden, for a slaughter sign is not a sign to rely upon.
mechaber.7#main: If one sent via a non-Jew without a seal, if that place is a public thoroughfare it is permitted, for he will fear lest one of the passersby see him and seize him as a thief; however, l'chatchila one should not send via a non-Jew without a seal.
mechaber.8#main: One who buys meat and sends it in the hand of an am ha'aretz is believed regarding it even though he is not established in kashrut, and we are not concerned that perhaps he switched it; and even Israelite slaves (°) and their mothers are believed in this matter. And some say that if he is suspect to eat things that the public is not accustomed to be lenient about, he is also suspect to switch.
mechaber.9#main: Meat found in the hand of a non-Jew with a seal or "kosher" written on it—even though one does not know who wrote it—is kosher, for it is known that it belongs to an Israelite; and this is when non-Jews who know how to write are not found there: {Rama: And likewise it is permitted to buy cheeses stamped the way Israelites stamp them (Mordekhai, chapter 8 of Avodah Zarah); and this is specifically in a place where there is no concern that perhaps the stamps remained in the hands of non-Jews and they affixed them on their cheeses (Or Zarua and Arukh). And some forbid in all of this since we do not know who wrote or sealed them (Mahariq, end of root 33); and b'dieved one should not be stringent.}
mechaber.10#main: One who leaves a non-Jew in his house and there are things in it that, if switched, involve even a Torah prohibition—if he goes out and comes in, or even if he stayed a long time and did not inform him that he intends to stay, it is permitted and we are not concerned that perhaps he switched, even if he benefits from switching; and this is when he did not lock the house on him (Tur and Mechaber, siman 129)—because he fears at every moment, saying, "Now he will come and see me." But if he informed him that he intends to stay, it is forbidden; and if he does not benefit from switching, it is permitted in every case, for we are not concerned that perhaps he switched to cause him to stumble, since he has no benefit in the matter.
mechaber.11#main: An Israelite and a non-Jew who set two pots one next to the other—this one with slaughtered meat and that one with nevelah—it is permitted, and we are not concerned that perhaps when the Israelite turned away the non-Jew switched slaughtered for nevelah, even if the Israelite's was superior; and even if their mouths are open it is permitted, and we are not concerned that perhaps sparks will fly from one to the other (and the same applies to two things roasted one next to the other (Mordekhai, chapter 8 of Avodah Zarah); but l'chatchila one should be careful even with two pots) (Tur).
mechaber.12#main: One should be stringent not to leave the pots with the maidservants when no Israelite is in the house: {Rama: And this is not the case of going out and coming in (responsum of the Rosh, klal 19); and if a mishap occurred and she put forbidden food in the pot, one should not feed her that food so as not to accustom her to this (Beit Yosef in the name of Shibolei HaLeket).}
mechaber.13#main: An Israelite who made cheeses in the house of a non-Jew and stamped them with a wooden stamp seal and forgot the stamp in the house of the non-Jew—we are not concerned that perhaps the non-Jew forged and sealed others with that same stamp; and likewise we are not concerned that perhaps the non-Jew smeared the faces of the cheeses with pig fat: {Rama: And some say that one should not permit if he forgot the stamp in the house of the non-Jew unless he left it resting on the cheeses that the Israelite made; but if he did not leave it so, and there is concern that perhaps he made small cheeses and switched them for large ones or for better ones, it is forbidden (Arukh, rule 47, law 2); and in a place of loss one may permit in every case.}

nekudot-hakesef.1#_: (Siman 118, Taz, s.k. 3) Therefore one should wonder at Or Zarua the Arukh, etc.—it is difficult for me: even though for Rabbenu Tam certainly a lock alone suffices, nevertheless we do not rely on him except with one seal—and this is the Rama's view, as the Shach wrote, s.k. 21; and we find similarly in many places.
nekudot-hakesef.2#_: (There, s.k. 4) And in my humble opinion all agree, etc.—and what will he do with meat and a piece of fish? (And in truth the Taz meant only wine, as the Derech Mitzvot emended.)
nekudot-hakesef.3#_: (There, s.k. 5) And the Levush wrote, etc.—and it is not so, etc.—it is difficult for me, for the Levush wrote thus for the law, and the same for us where there is concern he touched by way of being occupied, as below siman 128.
nekudot-hakesef.4#_: (There, s.k. 11) I wonder greatly, etc.—it is difficult for me: specifically there, where it is only cut as an Israelite cuts it, is there concern in meat found in a non-Jew's hand; but here there is a seal or "kosher" written on it, which clearly indicates it is kosher—if so, if he learned afterward of a treifah doubt he should have removed the seal or writing; moreover, it is not customary to give a seal or write "kosher" until it is known with certainty that it is kosher—and this is simple.

pitchei-teshuva.1#_: And milk and morayes—Pri Chadash (and brought in Ba'er Heitev, s.k. 2) wrote: even though impure milk is a Torah prohibition, nevertheless since pure milk is white and impure milk green, if he switched all or most it would be recognizable; therefore it is forbidden only d'rabbanan—for min b'mino is nullified in the majority d'oraisa, end of his words. One may wonder: behold the Shach above, siman 98, s.k. 6, concludes we follow taste—and therefore impure milk differs in taste from pure milk and requires sixty d'oraisa; and I found in responsum Noda Biyehudah, second series, Orach Chaim, siman 66, who also wondered at this and answered: because the rule that d'oraisa we learn from sheretz or gentile utensils applies only to prohibitions like them that are negative commandments with lashes, but not to negative commandments without lashes such as impure milk and the like—we do not say taste like substance from the Torah, only d'rabbanan forbidden—see there.
pitchei-teshuva.2#_: From the words of the scribes—see in responsum Mahari HaLevi, siman 14, who wrote that if one sent butter in a non-Jew's hand it is permitted even without a seal—see there; and so his brother the Taz wrote in his name below, siman 127, s.k. 7.
pitchei-teshuva.3#_: One seal—see in responsum Shemesh Tzedakah, Yoreh Deah, siman 15: they asked about one who sent his fellow from city to city via a non-Jew neck portions of geese filled with meat in one box with nails driven in without any seal—only on each a tag saying Pesach, which is not fit to be called a seal—what is their law: are the nails considered a seal so we can be lenient b'dieved as the Rama's view that via a non-Jew one seal suffices? He answered to permit in great loss and joined several reasons to be lenient and say the nails count as a seal even for a d'oraisa prohibition; and he wrote he presented the matter before the Rav Maharar Yosef Piemonte, who added another reason: because the Shulchan Aruch writes below, seif 5, if sent via a non-Jew a thigh without a seal cut, etc.—the same here, for certainly non-Jews do not make such things, and all agree b'dieved permitted with any seal, even without a seal; nevertheless to fence, etc., if not great loss. In my opinion it is difficult to rely on this alone where he sent without any seal at all, even in great loss—for even though non-Jews do not usually make such things, since they can easily do so it is like slaughter, which is not a sign to rely on, as below seif 6—and understand this.
pitchei-teshuva.4#_: The seal is damaged—see in responsum Noda Biyehudah, Yoreh Deah, siman 38.
pitchei-teshuva.5#_: Writing is not a sign—see in Magen Avraham, commentary 32, s.k. 13.
pitchei-teshuva.6#_: [And the like—Ba'er Heitev wrote that this includes a chicken in which nikkur of the neck tendons is recognizable as Israelites do, as above siman 68, seif 3, in the hagahah; for non-Jews do not do so but pluck in hot water; and there was an incident with a goose before singeing that a minister's slave took for tax and after two hours returned it to the owners and no sign was recognizable on it—and he also permitted by a sign in the feathers on the wing tips: three good feathers for writing missing from each wing, as is customary in all Jewish communities that the slaughterer plucks them immediately after slaughter—and understand.]
pitchei-teshuva.7#_: One should not feed her—Ba'er Heitev; and see in Sefer Tiferet Moshe who wrote there is a distinction: if she put it in to anger her, forbidden to feed even other non-Jews; but if for her pleasure, permitted to feed other non-Jews, for her intent was not fulfilled—end of his words.

rabbi-akiva-eiger-yd.1#_: (Siman 118, Shach, s.k. 8) That d'oraisa min b'mino is nullified—in Minchat Kohen on Menachot (folio 22) he brought a challenge in the name of Baal Imrei Emet, the Gaon R' Meir Fischles, may his memory be blessed: if so, what does the Gemara challenge on Rav from what he said about cheese from milk—for according to his view min b'mino is not nullified, it would be milk, a d'oraisa prohibition—and understand; see there. Also this is the Shach's conclusion above (siman 98): the matter of nullification in the majority depends on taste—if so, here it would be not its species, for impure and pure liver do not have the same taste; and see responsum Noda Biyehudah (Mahadura Tinyana, siman 66).

siftei-kohen.1#א: ["And meat, etc.—it implies that requiring seal within seal for meat is even where slaughterers are Israelite; and it is difficult regarding what the Taz wrote in siman 1, seif 4, that one who finds his animals and chickens properly slaughtered in the market is permitted because of majority of Israelite slaughterers—for there we do not know who slaughtered, therefore we follow the majority; but here, meat in a non-Jew's hand, we say he switched it with nevelah he had; and so the Mechaber in siman 63, seif 1—and the Sages already forbade all meat found in a non-Jew's hand even if all sellers and slaughterers are Israelite, end of his words. However, there is difficulty: the Rav wrote there at the end of the siman that if meat was in a non-Jew's hand where most sellers are Israelites it is kosher—perhaps here it deals where most sellers are not Israelites; and it seems to distinguish: there it deals only with meat found in a non-Jew's hand that they bought from the market, therefore where sellers are Israelites we permit, for no concern he bought nevelah, and no concern he switched with nevelah in his house—for what purpose would he switch, it is all his; but here, sending or depositing with a non-Jew, there is concern he switched with nevelah he still has; and one can further distinguish between sender or depositor where meat stays long in his hand and he has opportunity for nevelah and to switch, versus buying from the market; and as the Taz wrote in siman 128 regarding a ger toshav: forbidden to leave wine with him a long time, permitted a short time—for the same reason, no concern of switching in short time—see there; and see seif 6 and what is written there."]
siftei-kohen.1#ב: ["And a piece of fish, etc.—specifically a piece of fish; for a whole fish or half would be recognizable by fin and scale, as above siman 83."]
siftei-kohen.1#ג: ["Deposited or sent, etc.—it seems likewise l'chatchila permitted to send or deposit Torah-forbidden things with seal within seal and rabbinically forbidden things with one seal; and so the Mechaber wrote explicitly below, siman 130—it is simple."]
siftei-kohen.1#ד: ["In the hand of a non-Jew—not specifically; the same applies to a suspect Israelite who eats things the public are not accustomed to be lenient about, as the Mechaber writes in this siman, seif 8, and siman 119 (and see Rav HaMaggid, chapter 8 of Mishneh Torah, law 10, and understand). Rather, he mentioned non-Jew here because wine applies only with a non-Jew—for the reason for wine is affection of libation, he troubles and forges, as in s.k. 5—and this does not apply to a suspect Israelite unless he is suspect to libate wine for idolatry, then he is like a full non-Jew, as siman 119, s.k. 15; or he did not mention suspect Israelite because of cheese and the like, a matter the public are lenient about, as will be explained in s.k. 15. That he did not mention suspect to switch is obvious—understand."]
siftei-kohen.1#ה: ["But cooked wine, etc., and everything whose prohibition is from the scribes, etc.—the Mechaber's view: everything depends on whether forbidden from the Torah or rabbinically—for meat, concern he switched with nevelah, and fish with impure fish, which are Torah prohibitions; and wine, even though stam yeinam is only d'rabbanan, as below siman 123, nevertheless the Rashba wrote that because of affection of libation they trouble and forge even with one seal, therefore they were stringent like Torah; but cooked wine, beer, etc.—all those, even if switched, involve only rabbinic prohibition, as will be explained; since there is one seal we are not concerned for forgery—this is the Rambam's and Rashba's view (and R' Yerucham, end of 55). But the Ran wrote in the name of the Yerushalmi: the reason for wine, meat, and fish needing seal within seal is because the prohibition is intrinsic; but chamfig, where the prohibition is only through mixture, as explained in siman 114 and 115—and bread, though bread itself is forbidden, nevertheless because the prohibition is rabbinic, one seal suffices, end of his words; and so the Ra'ah in Bedek HaBayit, folio 118. He also holds that vinegar, since unfit for libation, we are not concerned he troubles and switches, since stam yeinam is d'rabbanan; wine is different because of affection of libation—he troubles and forges, as I will write in s.k. 6—for the Mechaber and his supporters; and so explicit from the Ran. It must be that the Ran and supporters hold milk and cheese are not called rabbinic prohibition here since there is concern for Torah-prohibited mixture—and understand. Rashi explained the reason: for chavivta their value is dear, he troubles and forges with one seal, unlike other things. I elaborated because the Rav in Torat Chatas, klal 32, law 14, wrote it is good to be stringent like all explanations; also in Simanei Torat Chacham he wrote many reasons for chavivta why seal within seal is needed, and everything similar that is Torah prohibition or rabbinic with intrinsic prohibition like chavivta, or rabbinic without intrinsic prohibition but considered like chavivta in every respect—needs seal within seal, end of his words; and so in Sefer Api Ravrevi. It is difficult why he stated here like the Mechaber, and why wonder greatly at Simanei Torat Chacham and Api Ravrevi: 'or rabbinic and its prohibition intrinsic'—for even for the Ran, in such a case one seal suffices like bread, as explicit in his words and the Ra'ah; perhaps one can say: specifically for bread, whose prohibition is rabbinic with no Torah root, as siman 112—we say so; but not for all other rabbinic prohibitions. And when he cited the Ran in Torat Chatas he added 'and bread even though its prohibition is intrinsic, nevertheless since its root is rabbinic, one seal suffices'—but the Ran is not in these words, and the Ran seems to hold even rabbinic prohibitions with a Torah root and intrinsic prohibition suffice with one seal, for he compared vinegar to bread, etc. See s.k. 7 and understand. Also, if so, he need not state the reason of wine because of affection of libation—for since it has a Torah root, it properly needs seal within seal—and understand."]
siftei-kohen.1#ו: ["And what the Mechaber wrote, 'such as honey'—he cited the Rambam's language; nevertheless in the Mechaber's words it must deal with mixing so much honey that the wine's taste changed, for then there is no stam yeinam, as below siman 123; but if only a little honey was mixed, the Mechaber holds there is stam yeinam concern, unlike the Rambam, as will be explained there; therefore in such a case one needs seal within seal here too—see below siman 130, seif 3 (and see responsum Mabit, part 2, siman 208)."]
siftei-kohen.1#ז: ["And what he wrote 'and likewise vinegar'—meaning vinegar of wine; and so explicit below siman 130, seif 3—it is when it bubbles as thrown on the ground, then it is full vinegar unfit for libation, as below siman 123, seif 6—see there. The reason: why concern—for affection of libation he troubles and forges? It is unfit for libation. If lest he switch with vinegar of libated wine—since stam yeinam is only d'rabbanan we are not concerned. The same for morayes, cooked wine, and wine mixed with other things—we are not concerned the non-Jew switches his morayes, cooked wine, and mixed wine, since all are forbidden only because of stam yeinam which is d'rabbanan—understand."]
siftei-kohen.1#ח: ["And milk, etc.—even though concern he switches with impure milk, a Torah prohibition, as explained in siman 1—it may be said impure milk is recognizable as turbid, as Avodah Zarah 35b: pure white, impure green; therefore no concern he switches all or most, only perhaps a little forbidden only d'rabbanan—for min b'mino is nullified d'oraisa, as siman 98; and so answered in Perishah, seif 4; and similarly Or Zarua, klal 48, end of law 5; or as Or Zarua, klal 45, law 7: since most milk among us is pure, stam milk is d'rabbanan. Bach on the Perishah wrote: they permitted him against his master who wrote against the Gemara and against Terumat HaDeshen the Arukh what did not occur to him—he thought milk has Torah prohibition; rather, one seal suffices because he has no profit—and so the Tur. It is reversed: he wrote against the Gemara and Terumat HaDeshen, and in the Tur it is explicit per the correct text in old books, which he agreed to: for milk one seal suffices since the prohibition is rabbinic, as the Rambam, Mechaber, and R' Yerucham, and Or Zarua in many places. But certainly, as with fish and other things he has profit switching pure for impure, so with milk—unless we come to 'he has no profit,' as the Taz wrote in this siman, seif 7 (from the Gemara and all poskim): we are not concerned he switched unless he benefits from switching—for whoever does not benefit is permitted even without any seal. The main point is as I wrote."]
siftei-kohen.1#ט: ["And morayes—also concern he switches with their morayes, forbidden where they put wine in it, as the Taz in siman 114, seif 1; but where they do not put wine, or wine is dearer than morayes, clearly no seal needed; and so the Mechaber there."]
siftei-kohen.1#י: ["And bread—only concern he switches with their bread, rabbinically forbidden, as siman 112; therefore where they practice leniency with non-Jewish bread, clearly no seal needed."]
