siftei-kohen.1#כ: ["And cheese—even though concern he switched with their cheese forbidden because they curdle with nevelah stomach lining, as the Taz in siman 115, seif 2—nevertheless d'oraisa the nevelah lining is nullified in minority; what is never nullified is d'rabbanan since it is a curdling agent, as above siman 87; or even if known they curdled with herbs or other things it is forbidden, as the Mechaber in siman 115—a rabbinic decree; or mainly: since we can say perhaps he did not curdle with nevelah lining, and even so forbidden—for we say 'perhaps he curdled'—it is properly d'rabbanan—understand."]
siftei-kohen.1#ל: ["Deposited in a non-Jew's hand—and the same for sent—understand well."]
siftei-kohen.1#מ: ["And some say, etc.—and below siman 130 the Mechaber states the first view without a disputant—and understand."]
siftei-kohen.1#נ: ["And even the sender, if he informed, etc.—this follows the second view, unlike the first—understand well."]
siftei-kohen.1#ס: ["If he informed his fellow the form of the seal and also told the non-Jew, etc.—it seems what the Taz wrote: if he informed his fellow, etc., is not precise—for the same if he does not inform his fellow but tells the non-Jew he informed, he still fears, thinking it true; for the Taz wrote in seif 2: once sealed properly, etc., where one suffices one need not return to see—and it implies even per the 'some say' view that a depositor needs only one seal, they wrote so; and so the Rav in hagahah below siman 130, seif 2—the same for a sender who told the non-Jew he informed his fellow the seal's form: no need to return and see. Also, if with a sender one seal requires the recipient to return and see—what purpose informing the non-Jew? Since the fellow knows the seal's form and must return and see, he will see visually if forged or not—why is this worse than a depositor? Rather, the Taz teaches: when he informed his fellow the seal's form, it does not suffice until he also tells the non-Jew he informed him; and customarily when one tells the non-Jew so, he presumably informs. He wrote 'and also told the non-Jew' last, not the reverse. Nevertheless, even when sending with two seals it is proper to inform the fellow the seal's form so he will inspect, as the Taz in siman 130, end of seif 8—see there; perhaps therefore they also mentioned this when he informed the form—to say that in such a case one may do so l'chatchila."]
siftei-kohen.1#ע: ["Only for a suspect Israelite—for he is worse than a non-Jew in this matter, who is trusted they will believe him and does not fear much. It implies for meat, wine, and fish a suspect Israelite needs two seals, and for chamfig one seal. It implies per 'some say' there is no distinction between depositor and sender. 'Suspect Israelite' means suspect to switch—not suspect to eat what he sends, for we hold one suspect to eat forbidden things is not suspect to switch; perhaps those things the public are not lenient about—he is also suspect to switch if suspect to eat them, as the Mechaber in seif 8 and siman 119. But the Rashba wrote eating non-Jewish cheese is lenient in the public's eyes; and so Torat HaBayit; and Beit Yosef brings it in siman 119; and the Tur in siman 119: one suspect regarding cheese is not suspect to switch—and so from the poskim; see siman 119, s.k. 52."]
siftei-kohen.2#א: ["One need not return to see it—the reason: seals are only because presumably he does not trouble and forge—see s.k. 15."]
siftei-kohen.2#ב: ["Even if he made two seals—and likewise more; and below siman 130, seif 8, the Rav set conditions on this—see there."]
siftei-kohen.2#ג: ["Concern he forbade through contact—meaning even if he did not benefit, concern because of affection of libation he touched it—see below siman 128, s.k. 4."]
siftei-kohen.2#ד: ["Even though the seal is damaged—apparently made intentionally by a person; if not, permitted in every case, as below siman 130, s.k. 6 and 8 in the hagahah."]
siftei-kohen.3#_: One letter counts as one seal—it implies even for things where one seal suffices, one letter counts as a sign and is better than a lock, as the Mechaber wrote in the next seif.
siftei-kohen.4#_: But for things where one seal suffices, etc.—this means chamfig and the like; and it seems per the 'some say' view, for a depositor one does not need even for chavivta except one seal; and so the 'some say' view that with a non-Jew everything is permitted with a seal, as above seif 1—a lock is not counted as one seal. The Rav wrote in siman 130, seif 2, and siman 131, seif 1: libated wine in a non-Jew's hand b'dieved suffices with one seal—and he did not write more leniency that b'dieved even one lock suffices, because he stated here like the Mechaber, meaning as I explained; and even though for Rabbenu Tam certainly one lock suffices, nevertheless we do not rely on him except with one seal—and in Bach he wrote here and in siman 130 that b'dieved even one lock suffices, and so the Rav's view—see there—it is not clear. Also what he brought as proof from the Rashba's responsum in the Mordekhai, chapter R' Yishmael, and from the Rashba's responsum () klal 19, siman 3, for this law—I rejected all in my books; truly the construction, see there. Also his distinguishing against the Mechaber in chamfig, that it is permitted even l'chatchila with one lock—I do not see in his words grounds to dispute, since the Rashba and Taz agreed that specifically one seal is needed even b'dieved; especially since they said to be stringent.
siftei-kohen.5#א: ["If sent via a non-Jew, etc.—kosher—the language implies somewhat b'dieved only for nikkur and the like; but not l'chatchila. The Tur also wrote in this language; nevertheless the Mechaber wrote explicitly in siman 65 that it is permitted even l'chatchila via a non-Jew with a nikkur sign; but the Mechaber wrote nothing of this there; nevertheless Or Zarua wrote l'chatchila one should not rely on it; and so the Rav in Simanei Torat Chacham there."]
siftei-kohen.5#ב: ["But if he sent a d'rabbanan prohibition, etc.—explained in Torat HaBayit there: for d'rabbanan prohibition, even if a Jew saw the seal was completely broken and clearly the seal was opened—it is permitted in this matter; and so in Torat Chatas there, law 14—see there."]
siftei-kohen.6#א: ["Forbidden—the reason: perhaps the non-Jew switched good for bad and slaughtered himself for the one he switched; and slaughter is not a sign to rely on. Perishah, seif 11: specifically where there is no majority of Israelites or majority of Israelite slaughterers—therefore we concern he switched with nevelah and do not rely on a slaughter sign; unlike above siman 1, where there is majority of Israelites and slaughterers we rely on the majority found at slaughter who are experts, end of his words. It is difficult—for the Taz seems to deal here even where majority of slaughterers and Israelites are Israelite; and so explicit in Rokeach, siman 406, and Bach's last pamphlet: specifically here we concern he switched to profit and slaughtered himself for the one he switched; but if his kids and chickens were lost and found slaughtered—they are kosher and we are not concerned a non-Jew slaughtered them, for since he recognizes them as his and they were not switched, no concern a non-Jew slaughtered for profit since he has no benefit, and presumably Israelites slaughtered them, and most found at slaughter are experts, end of his words. I did not grasp his view—for it seems explicit in those cases (folio 24b) that even one who finds a slaughtered animal not his is permitted with majority of Israelites; and so the Tur, seif 11; and as explained in siman 63. The Mechaber in siman 1, seif 4 wrote 'if his kids were lost'—he stated it as common usage, or the Mechaber follows his view that meat lost from sight is forbidden in siman 63, therefore he requires specifically his kids that he recognizes as his; unlike us who hold meat lost from sight is permitted. It seems clear there is no dispute with siman 1—for there it was never in a non-Jew's hand, only we did not know who slaughtered, therefore we follow the majority; but here, sending via a non-Jew, concern he switched good for bad, therefore even where majority of Israelites are found we concern he slaughtered himself for profit for the one he switched; and this is unlike meat found in a non-Jew's hand permitted with majority of Israelites, as above s.k. 1—see there."]
siftei-kohen.6#ב: ["For a slaughter sign is not a sign to rely on. Mordekhai, responsum 378, brought by Beit Yosef, siman 63: an incident—a slaughtered chicken sent via a non-Jew without a guard; they doubted perhaps another was switched; they asked the slaughterer if he slaughtered this chicken; he answered: I have no visual recognition; however now I slaughtered one chicken; but the owner recognized it and said this is it, and I permitted it since the owner recognized it, end of his words; and so Maharshal, first chapter of Chullin, siman 23, and responsum 378; and he added: but if they did not ask the slaughterer, it is not a sign, end of his words—and it is simple."]
siftei-kohen.7#_: If sent via a non-Jew without a seal, etc.—implies even with other non-Jews who are not his slave and maidservant, permitted b'dieved if that place is a public thoroughfare; and so in Torat Chatas there, law 15—not like Or Zarua who permitted only his slave and maidservant.
siftei-kohen.8#א: ["And even Israelite slaves, etc.—the Rav HaMaggid explained: Canaanite slaves who were circumcised and immersed for slavery—and they are like women, end of his words—see below siman 124, seif 3, and siman 267."]
siftei-kohen.8#ב: ["He is also suspect to switch—in siman 119 it will be explained: specifically for that thing he is suspect to eat, he is also suspect to switch—see there."]
siftei-kohen.9#א: ["And likewise permitted to buy cheese, etc.—this is all the more from meat, which the Mechaber wrote is d'oraisa; the Rav wrote only because of the end."]
siftei-kohen.9#ב: ["And b'dieved, etc.—meaning if he already bought from the non-Jew; and it seems it deals where there is no concern stamps remained with non-Jews, etc., only we do not know who wrote or sealed; but where there is concern stamps remained with non-Jews and they affixed them on their cheeses—forbidden even b'dieved; see responsum Avnei Nezer, part 3, siman 1. However, the Atzei Chayim wrote at the end of the siman: in great loss one may permit even in such a case b'dieved; see end of siman and what is written there. He wrote in Torat Chatas, klal 81, law 4: the custom is to buy wines non-Jews bring from the land called Muscovy via their seals, for they bring writings from Israel, end of his words; and so in Simanei Torat Chacham there: for wine they practice leniency—see below siman 130, seif 6."]
siftei-kohen.10#א: ["One who leaves, etc.—in Chullin 3a he derives from the language 'one who leaves' that it is b'dieved; however the Gemara concludes there that even l'chatchila permitted with going out and coming in; therefore what the Tur wrote this language is because of the end: he stayed long and did not inform he intends to stay, which is permitted only b'dieved; and so the Rav below siman 129, seif 1—forbidden l'chatchila in such a case—see there; this is from the Mordekhai, chapter R' Yishmael, in the name of Ra'avan; or as Tosafot in Chullin there: 'one who leaves' also implies l'chatchila."]
siftei-kohen.10#ב: ["If he goes out and enters, etc.—it seems even a child going out and entering helps, as above siman 115, seif 1 in the hagahah (and even for a d'oraisa prohibition—and see responsum of the Rashba that Beit Yosef brought in siman 130 regarding relying on minors' guarding, etc.), as the Mechaber writes in siman 69, seif 10, regarding rinsing—see there. Even though one could say there is different because blood he cooked does not absorb, and there is only rabbinic prohibition, as Maharshal permits with non-Jew who rinsed and as explained in Beit Yosef and Torat Chatas, end of klal 41—it seems specifically for reliability one can distinguish: for d'oraisa prohibition he is not believed with non-Jewish rinsing except a woman's testimony; but for fear there is no distinction."]
siftei-kohen.10#ג: ["And when he did not lock the house on him—he does not mean one must know he did not lock; but from presumption it is forbidden unless it became known it was locked—for in Avodah Zarah 69b it is explicit that from presumption we are not concerned he locked the door; rather he means it was not known the door was locked; and so explicit in siman 129, seif 1—see there."]
siftei-kohen.11#א: ["And we are not concerned that when he turned away, etc.—he fears lest the Israelite turn back immediately and see him; and from the Rosh's responsum, klal 19, siman 18, it is proven that even with non-Jew and Israelite guests we are not concerned—for what we permit with going out and entering is even with guests who do not know each other, for they also fear each other—see there; and so in Tosafot's rulings, first chapter of Avodah Zarah, siman 12, from Tosafot there, beginning folio 12—and see siman 88, seif 2."]
siftei-kohen.11#ב: ["One should be careful even with two pots—meaning because of sparks; and since he wrote 'even,' when mouths are not open one need not be careful with two pots—see the s.k. after it at the end."]
siftei-kohen.12#א: ["And he does not go out and enter—the Rav's view seems that with going out and entering one need not be stringent; at first glance in the Rosh and Tur it does not seem so—for after writing the law of two pots as the Mechaber in seif 11, they wrote: on this we rely to leave pots with maidservants when going to synagogue, which is like going out and entering; and it is fit for God-fearing to be stringent, for mishaps occurred many times; and also to improve her portion she puts milk in the pot, end of his words (and see in the Rosh himself)—it seems even with going out and entering one should be stringent. What the Rav learned from the Rosh's responsum that if an Israelite goes out and enters it is permitted—in the responsum his view for the law is permitted, for he wrote there: as we say in the first chapter of Avodah Zarah, you did not go to Tyre all your days and see a non-Jew and Israelite who set two pots, etc.; and in his rulings, first chapter of Avodah Zarah, he wrote on this 'you went to Tyre,' meaning for the law; but it is fit for God-fearing to be stringent, see there. But the Mechaber who wrote 'one should be stringent,' etc., as the Rosh in his rulings 'and fit for God-fearing to be stringent,' etc.—even with going out and entering he speaks; and one can say the Rav understood from the Rosh's not answering the questioner there that l'chatchila one should be stringent even with going out and entering—therefore with going out and entering there is not even a stringency; and what he wrote 'fit for God-fearing,' etc., applies when going to synagogue, because he does not hold going out and entering applies since they stay in synagogue a while and maidservants know they stay; but with actual going out and entering one need not be stringent (and see siman 113, seif 4). Do not challenge from the previous seif that l'chatchila one should be careful even with two pots—it is simple that Israelite and non-Jew who set pots is no worse than going out and entering, for there the reason is sparks that fly, as in the previous s.k."]
siftei-kohen.12#ב: ["And if a mishap occurred, etc.—forbidden food in the pot, etc.—in Shibolei HaLeket it is written she put forbidden food in the pot to anger, etc.; and so the Rav cited in Torat Chatat, klal 32, law 9; here the word 'to anger' was omitted because it is not precise—one reason he wrote: so they not learn to do so, applies also if her intent was for their pleasure; he mentioned 'to anger' to exclude if she did not know that thing she put in the pot was forbidden to an Israelite—and this means she put forbidden food in the pot to anger, meaning she knew that thing was forbidden to an Israelite and nevertheless gave it. He also wrote in Beit Yosef in the name of Shibolei HaLeket: a non-Jew who said do not eat from this pot, for I threw milk in it—we do not accept from him, rather it is permitted, end of his words; and so the Rav in Torat Chatas, klal 32, law 9—and he wrote this is simple from the case of a non-Jew bringing fruit to market: a non-Jew is not believed neither for prohibition nor permission—see siman 122, seif 3, and siman 127."]
siftei-kohen.12#ג: ["One should not feed her that food, etc.—in Shibolei HaLeket: not to that non-Jew nor other non-Jews; and so in Torat Chatas and Simanei Torat Chacham there; here the Rav wrote 'one should not feed her' without qualification—it must be he does not argue."]
siftei-kohen.13#א: ["We are not concerned, etc.—the non-Jew will fear the Jew is accustomed to make his stamp in a special place; also lest the Israelite notice because the later ones made afterward are softer; also there are many doubts—for perhaps the lost stamp never came to the non-Jew's hand; and if it came, perhaps he did not forge; and if he forged, perhaps he only stamped with something permitted, end of Mordekhai. The first two reasons do not suffice except for those cheeses the Israelite left in the non-Jew's house; the last reason suffices also to buy other cheeses from him—see seif 9 in the hagahah and what is written there."]
siftei-kohen.13#ב: ["And likewise we are not concerned he smeared, etc.—for we are not concerned he intended to cause stumbling as long as the non-Jew has no benefit in the matter, as in seif 10—and see seif 2 in the hagahah."]
siftei-kohen.13#ג: ["But if he did not leave it so—meaning even if he left it elsewhere in a special place intentionally, nevertheless since he did not leave it resting on the cheeses, the non-Jew thinks the Israelite does not know where he left it—and forbidden."]

turei-zahav.1#א: Requires two seals. In the Tur he wrote the reason in the name of Rashi: for wine, meat, and fish (chavivta) two seals are required, and for cheese, bread, and wine (chamfig) one seal—for chavivta their value is dear, and for wine because of the affection of libation; according to this it is specifically those. But the Rashba attributes the reason that for chavivta there is concern for a d'oraisa prohibition, and for chamfig a d'rabbanan prohibition, and he counts cheese among them. The Derishah challenged: behold milk is also a d'oraisa prohibition through substitution of impure milk—and he answered that the mixture is d'rabbanan.
turei-zahav.1#ב: Only for a suspect Israelite—for he is worse than a non-Jew, who is trusted that they will believe him and he does not fear so much; and even though in siman 86 the Tur wrote in the name of the Rambam that a non-Jew is worse than an Israelite not established in kashrut, there in any case he is not suspect with certainty, whereas here "suspect" means in something the public are careful about, as stated in seif 8.
turei-zahav.1#ג: But with a non-Jew everything is permitted, etc.—for Tosafot challenge: here we say regarding wine, which is among chavivta, that two seals are required, and above in that chapter we say the halachah is like R' Eliezer who said a lock and seal—and some texts read a lock or seal, which suffices; therefore Rabbenu Tam answered that there regarding chavivta it deals with a suspect Israelite, and above with a non-Jew. Tosafot challenged him and explained that there is a distinction between a messenger and one who deposits, as the Shulchan Aruch writes nearby; and in the text of R' Eliezer that I cited there is a distinction—for Rabbenu Tam's text reads "or seal," and the Rashba reads "and seal," and according to him a lock is not a seal at all where only one seal is needed, but only where two seals are needed does a lock help in combination, as the Shulchan Aruch writes in seif 4. Now, according to what the Rama wrote here, following Or Zarua, that b'dieved one may rely on Rabbenu Tam and permit sending via a non-Jew with one seal—from that, a lock alone is also permitted according to his text that reads "lock or seal"; and if so, when the Shulchan Aruch wrote in seif 4 that for things where one seal suffices a lock does not help, the Rama should have written on it that b'dieved a lock helps, for one reason is that since we rely on Rabbenu Tam we rely on this too, for one depends on the other; therefore one should wonder at Or Zarua, who in klal 22 ruled to permit b'dieved like Rabbenu Tam, as the Rama rules here, and afterward wrote in the name of the Tur that a lock is not like one seal—and it may be that he wrote this for l'chatchila, but b'dieved certainly a lock suffices, and so explained Mahari Cohen; yet he brought proof from the Mordekhai, chapter R' Yishmael, and I wonder greatly on this, for perhaps the reason is that he fears being seized as a thief on wine even if the inn is locked, since if the Jew came he would fear like a thief, etc.—but Mahari Cohen's explanation that "and the keys in their hands" means in the Jews' hands is not correct; rather it means in the guards' hands, as the Mordekhai explains in the chapter HaSocher in this incident that R' Chaim Cohen wrote explicitly "even if he gave him the key," etc.; therefore one must rely on the non-Jew's fear, but truly if it were in a Jew's hand it would be permitted because of a seal according to Rabbenu Tam; so it seems clearly that Mahari Cohen intended the law, and the Rama abbreviated where he should have written the leniency for us b'dieved in seif 4.
turei-zahav.1#ד: And b'dieved one may rely on this—so too Or Zarua, klal 26; also in Tosafot (folio 69) it is so; and in my opinion it seems that all agree (regarding wine) [in this time] that the main reason we are concerned with wine requiring two seals, even though it is d'rabbanan, is because of the affection of libation wine, as I wrote in seif 1; and in our time they are not idol worshippers, as written below—therefore the affection of libation does not apply, and all agree that one seal suffices.
turei-zahav.2#_: Or it is wine and there is concern, etc.—this matter is puzzling, for certainly he benefits from switching—he will drink from it and add water; and in this one certainly cannot say that he sees the wine is good as at first, for it is forbidden to taste it; only for meat can one say so, that its appearance is fatty and good, but not for something that depends on taste. It seems his meaning regarding wine is that even if it is clear to us that he did not drink from it—e.g., guards outside prevented bringing water to mix—and we see nothing missing from its measure—still there is concern because of contact, even though he does not benefit; especially in a barrel or wide cup there is concern that while occupied he touched the wine, as the Rama wrote in siman 128, seif 4; and the Levush wrote the reason is affection of libation, which is not so, for then it should be permitted for us, which it is not; and so Or Zarua, klal 22, in the name of Semag.
turei-zahav.4#א: But for things where one seal suffices, etc.—I already wrote in seif 1 that for us it is kosher b'dieved with a lock even where only one seal is needed.
turei-zahav.4#ב: And also the sack—meaning that he sealed the sack as well.
turei-zahav.5#א: If he sent via a non-Jew a thigh, etc.—it implies specifically b'dieved, but l'chatchila not; and so Or Zarua, klal 22; and it is explained in our words in siman 63 in the name of the Mordekhai that whenever one has a ta'am in what he sent via the non-Jew, it is permitted.
turei-zahav.5#ב: Any piece in which Israelite nikkur is recognizable, etc.—it seems obvious that this includes a chicken in which nikkur of the neck tendons is recognizable as Israelites do, on which one may rely for permission.
turei-zahav.7#א: A public thoroughfare, etc.—meaning even where Jews are not commonly found but only non-Jews—this non-Jew fears lest other non-Jews see him and tell the Israelite, as the Tur and Shulchan Aruch write in siman 129, seif 4.
turei-zahav.7#ב: However, l'chatchila, etc.—in Torat Chatas, klal 32, he wrote that the custom is to send via a non-Jew in a place that is a public thoroughfare and is an Israelite neighborhood where non-Jews are not found, etc.—for it is known that it belongs to an Israelite. I wonder greatly: behold there is concern that it was truly an Israelite's and he intended to eat it and made a sign to recognize it among other treifah pieces, and afterward he learned this one was treifah; and the Rashba himself wrote this reasoning elsewhere in Mishmeret HaBayit (folio 118, end of column 2); and Tosafot wrote it in chapter 3 (folio 94), regarding if a non-Jew cut at the place of the gid—we are concerned perhaps afterward he learned it was treifah and therefore sent it to another non-Jew for nikkur, etc.; whence do we not concern ourselves here, and we are lenient in a d'oraisa doubt?
turei-zahav.11#_: One should be careful even with two pots—in D.M. in the name of the Mordekhai, chapter Ein Ma'amidin; the reason is lest they be switched one for the other, and he derives this from the chapter Keitzad Tzolin that one does not roast two Paschal lambs in one oven, even a kid and lamb, because of mixture of bodies; accordingly, if there are two Israelite pots, one of meat and one of milk, there is no prohibition even l'chatchila to cook them in one oven, since switching does not apply. Those who seek sources wrote that the Rama's words are in the Tur and it is an error: it is written in the Agudah, chapter 3, that once Jews were seized and the non-Jews took all they had; they were ransomed and returned, and found their pots in goose fat, and said they recognized them by sight as when they left them—it seems to me to permit, for it is no worse than visual recognition of a vessel; and it is also in the Mordekhai, chapter Ein Ma'amidin, that when an Israelite gives a non-Jew a cooked dish in a pot to bring to the non-Jew's house, the Israelite should warn him not to wash the bowl but leave some residue of the food, and likewise bring it back the same day, etc. One may wonder how he relies on telling the non-Jew to leave food residue—perhaps he will use it and then return and put food residue in it. Mahari Cohen cited a responsum of Maharar Menachem of Cordova left among non-Jews: an Israelite had already taken a little fat from the pot with a spoon, and when the pot was returned with the fat he recognized the depression in the fat from which fat was taken—it seems to permit, for in such a case visual recognition applies, etc.

yad-ephraim.1#_: Wine and meat—Ba'er Heitev and responsa Shevut Yaakov, siman 72: communities that slaughter at non-Jews' place, gentile animals via seal as required—even though for stam yeinam if the wine is a non-Jew's two seals do not help and one must sit and guard—here there is only concern of switching, which we do not concern ourselves about since he has no profit: if an Israelite sees it is not as fatty as the meat he left he will not take it; and moreover he troubled himself and spent expenses, and slaughtering somewhat consumes the hide— in such a case we are not concerned, as written in siman 131; see there.
yad-ephraim.2#_: If it had only a lock—Ba'er Heitev and responsa Chavot Yair, siman 39 at the end, objects to the Peri Chadash who permits leaving cooked food in a non-Jew's oven for Shabbat honor for a day and night with a lock alone—for this is not like a craftsman and merchant where one lock is nothing, since even if he returns and sees it what can he recognize in a lock; and mainly in the pot itself there cannot be a sign regarding large and small, and even regarding fat, for it shrinks all night and he can evade; and he is not afraid to lose his craft, for they will think if he knows and they do not believe him they will seal with two seals—see there; and see Turei Zahav who mentioned this briefly.
yad-ephraim.3#_: And also the sack—Ba'er Heitev; and see Beit Yosef Chayei, siman 161, also for cheese.
yad-ephraim.4#_: A d'rabbanan prohibition—Ba'er Heitev; and in responsa Ginat Veradim, Yoreh Deah, klal 1, siman 19, regarding cheeses artisans make in villages and send via their non-Jewish servant to the province to an Israelite—no concern of switching, for he could also buy such cheese cheaply, and several other reasons—see there siman 20; and see more in responsa Pri HaAdamah, part 3, folio 80b: one who sent cheeses via an Ishmaelite non-Jew without a seal, only in a sewn sack, and the Israelite who gave it to him recognizes they are those, and also such cheese is not common (he noted they bring from there—no gentile cheese makers, only Israelites)—we do not concern ourselves that he switched; and also perhaps the whole load was in one place and he fears to switch—there is room to permit in great loss: throw away or sell to non-Jews two or three wheels alone—see there; his reason to throw or sell two seems that even if such cheeses are not common, perhaps forbidden cheeses came to his hand and he switched—therefore concern only on two or three; and we are not more concerned since there is only an Israelite artisan—see Beit Yosef Chayei, siman 162, Reuven sent, and more there siman 163.
yad-ephraim.5#_: A place of public thoroughfare—Ba'er Heitev; and responsa Shevut Yaakov, part 3, siman 74: one sent via a non-Jew fat from his estate, about half a measure, through a street of Jews—a public place—at first glance it seemed permitted even if the non-Jew stayed twenty-two hours and could switch, as in siman 118; but one can reject: perhaps only barrels, a defined item, and he is seized as a thief on them; but here he can excuse himself that a little spilled and he refills—and since he acts negligently without guarding, it is fit to forbid—see there; and responsa Tashbetz, siman 45: meat cooked as required and brought by a non-Jewish porter, with a sign or ta'am, and the porter is in the public domain where passersby are mostly Israelite, and it was Friday eve when the porter's house has Israelites—we are not concerned about switching since there is a sign or ta'am; and where Israelites pass anyway it is permitted; and for mixtures we are not concerned since the non-Jew has no benefit; and also where the public are found and at the edge of non-Jews we are not concerned since it is already like food of the court; nevertheless, to distance from ugliness to sanctify yourself in ethics—you did well, for so is the way of pious ones who are stringent for themselves and lenient for others—see there.
